item.title: Julio Mendoza Loor and Jewel’s Goldstrike capture Mexico World Cup Freestyle On Highest Score in 3 Years for American-based rider from Ecuador.
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Julio Mendoza Loor and Jewel’s Goldstrike captured the World Cup Grand Prix Freestyle Sunday with the highest score in three years for the American-based rider from Ecuador.

The post Julio Mendoza Loor and Jewel’s Goldstrike capture Mexico World Cup Freestyle On Highest Score in 3 Years for American-based rider from Ecuador. appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 25, 2026

Julio Mendoza Loor and Jewel’s Goldstrike captured the Mexico City World Cup Grand Prix Freestyle Sunday with the highest score in three years for the American-based rider from Ecuador.

Julio and the 15-year-old Dutch-bred gelding were awarded 80.605% a day after victory in the Grand Prix and the highest score for the duo based in Columbus, North Carolina since their gold medal performance at the 2023 Pan American Games.

Ecuador is not in any of the established World Cup regions such as North America so Julio will have to wait until near the end of qualifying to find out whether he tops other combinations in a similar situation to be among the total of 18 riders from around the world invited to the Final in Gothenburg, Sweden next March. Julio competed Goldstrike in the 2024 Olympics and this year’s World Championships as well as the World Cup Final in Fort Worth, Texas last April.

Patrik Kittel  of Sweden and the 14-year-old gelding Touchdown that won the World Cup title in 2024 scored 78.800% for runner-up, as the pair was in the Grand Prix. The points won in Mexico were enough to boost him near the top of the Western European League which so far has staged only one of 10 qualifiers this season.

Jennifer Williams, based in Wellington, Florida and the 12-year-old Dutch-bred gelding Joppe K was the highest placed of three North Americans in fourth on a score of 73.915%.

This was the first qualifying event this year for Jennifer and Joppe and gave the pair 20 points with seven more qualifiers in North America that gets to send three horse and rider combinations to the Final based on their three best results.

Kevin Kohmann also of Wellington on the American-bred Sonata MF was the third placed North American on 71.545%.

The 15 points earned in Mexico added to 20 for winning at Devon, Pennsylvania last month and enough to boost the rider and the mare to the top of the North American standings. Devon Kane, his wife, on Vamos is ranked second.

The next North American World Cup event is in Toronto Nov. 9-14.

item.title: Julio Mendoza Loor, USA-Based Ecuador Rider, and Jewel’s Goldstrike Win Mexico City World Cup Grand Prix, 2024 Champion Patrik Kittel & Touchdown 2nd
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Julio Mendoza Loor, USA-based Ecuador rider, and Jewel's Goldstrike win Mexico City World Cup Grand Prix while 2024 champion partnership of Patrik Kittel of Sweden and Touchdown runner-up

The post Julio Mendoza Loor, USA-Based Ecuador Rider, and Jewel’s Goldstrike Win Mexico City World Cup Grand Prix, 2024 Champion Patrik Kittel & Touchdown 2nd appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 24, 2026

Julio Mendoza Loor, the U.S.-based Ecuador rider, and Jewel’s Goldstrike won the Mexico City World Cup Grand Prix Saturday while 2024 champion partnership of Patrik Kittel of Sweden and Touchdown was runner-up.

Kevin Kohmann on the American-bred Sonata MF was the highest placed North American in third and on a campaign for the rider’s fourth straight World Cup Final.

Julio, based in Columbus, North Caroline and the 15-year-old Dutch-bred gelding that competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and this year’s World Championship’s in Aachen, Germany scored 73.891% as the unanimous choice of the five judges for the top spot on 73.891%.

Julio and Goldstrike scored more than two percentage points above Sweden’s Patrik Kittel and the 14-year-old gelding Touchdown that were awarded 71.804%. Patrik and his Swedish-bred mount were competing in the U.S. for the second time this year, havng shown at the World Cup Final in Fort Worth, Texas in April. The duo, with the 2024 Olympics, 2022 and 2026 World Championships, two European Championships won the World Cup in 2024.

Kevin Kohmann, based in Wellington, Florida rode Sonata MF, 11-year-old mare, placed third on 69.065%.

Kevin, who competed Dünensee in the three most recent World Cup Finals, began competing Sonata six months ago.

On the mare bred by Maryanna Haymon and owned by Diamante Farms, he won at the Devon, Pennsylvania World Cup qualifier last month. The duo currently stands second in North America, behind his wife, Devon Kane, on Vamos, but if he is the highest placed North American in Sunday’s Freestyle would jump to the top of the regional standings and give the pair with an opportunity to become one of three North Americans to qualify for the annual championship in Gothenburg, Sweden next March.

item.content:encoded:
The countdown for this year’s International Equestrian Federation (FEI) Awards began Wednesday Oct. 21  and is open until midnight Central European/6pm US Eastern time Nov. 1.

The public vote counts for 50% across the four categories: Peden Bloodstock FEI Best Athlete, Longines FEI Rising Star, Cavalor FEI Best Groom and FEI Inspire Award.

Votes can be cast at https://www.fei.org/awards.

There are seven official judges–none from the Americas.

item.title: Early Looks at New Dressage Tests Receive Positive Reviews
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Early Looks at new dressage tests receive positive reviews from American and German riders

The post Early Looks at New Dressage Tests Receive Positive Reviews appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 20, 2026

Early reviews of international dressage tests to be introduced for competitions beginning next Jan. 1 have received positive reviews from American and German riders.

“I actually like the idea of adding a stretching circle to the Grand Prix because I think we need to go back to the basics,” said Marcus Orlob who rode on the U.S. team at the 2024 Olympics, We ask so much collection from our horses at this level, but we also need to allow them to stretch, relax, and stay connected.

“I also think moving the collected walk to a different part of the test is a great idea. It gives the judges a much better opportunity to see the quality of the walk, the rhythm, and whether the horse maintains a clear four-beat walk without tension.

“For me, good dressage is about harmony and correct training, not just performing difficult movements. A horse should be able to show both collection and relaxation. Of course, we’ll have to see how the new test rides and how the judges score it, but overall I think these are positive changes that bring us back to the fundamentals of good dressage.”

The new for all international tests were prepared over the past year by the International Equestrian Federation (FEI) Dressage Test Writing Group and are available at https://inside.fei.org/fei/your-role/organisers/dressage/tests. The new tests to to “include movements that better demonstrate suppleness, balance and self-carriage” are a step in an overhaul of international dressage that will climax with proposed revisions of rules to be debated at the annual FEI General Assembly this year.

Katharina Hemmer, who was on Germany’s gold medal team at the World Championships in Aachen August rode the new version of the Grand Prix at a test event.

“For me it went well and fluent,” she said. “I don’t think it will be a problem for a classical trained horse to show the stretching in the test.”

Adrienne Lyle, three-time Olympian for USA and with an extensive training program, said: “I think it’s important as riders we are willing to embrace change and stay open-minded. Our training programs should focus on creating a proper connection where the horse stretches to the bit softly and willingly, so from a training perspective I welcome it. I know there is a lot of debate about the length of test and those ramifications so hopefully it can be evaluated honestly and see how it works, or doesn’t work, for that aspect of the sport, and make any changes necessary as we go.”

Kevin Kohmann based in Wellington and in pursuit of his fourth straight World Cup Final start, commented: “I do like the stretchy circle because it’s classical riding and it’s actually good for the horses to have people practice this more. My horses are all very good at it so it’s very good for me.

“The change of the walk I don’t think was really necessary but also for training purposes it’s better to walk longer before you passage than coming right out of the corner and having to passage.”

item.content:encoded:
Oct. 18, 2026

Quinn Iverson and Gremlin won the Grand Prix Special Sunday for a sweep of the TerraNova CDI3* and the third victory since beginning Big Tour seven months ago.

Quinn, based in Wellington, Florida, and the 11-year-old Oldenburg gelding scored 70.085% for the win, two days after capturing the Grand Prix two days ago. The duo posted the first international Grand Prix victory in Germany in August.

Nora Batchelder of Willison, Florida and the 11-year-old Oldenburg mare Nova was runner-up on 68.021%.

Eline Eckroth of Ocala on Ket to B Fabulous posted a personal best 62.468% in the return of the 11-year-old KWPN gelding after a brreak from international Grand Prix after four straight Medium Tour victories this year.

item.title: Devon Kane Rides Vamos to Personal Best Score for Victory at TerraNova World Cup Freestyle, Takes Over North American Lead from Husband Kevin Kohmann
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Devon Kane rides Vamos to personal best score for victory at TerraNova World Cup Freestyle, takes over North American lead from husband Kevin Kohmann

The post Devon Kane Rides Vamos to Personal Best Score for Victory at TerraNova World Cup Freestyle, Takes Over North American Lead from Husband Kevin Kohmann appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 17, 2026

Devon Kane rode Vamos to a personal best score to claim victory in the TerraNova World Cup Freestyle Saturday and take over the lead from her husband, Kevin Kohmann, in the North American standings after two of 10 qualifiers for the champinship Final.

Devon and the 14-year-old Westfalen gelding, owned by her family’s Diamante Farms in Wellington, Florida were awarded 75.505% for the win on Florida’s Gulf Coast. The win came a day after the Grand Prix also on a personal best.

The victory to earn 20 points adds to 10 won at Devon, Pennsylvania last month and drops her husband to second place in the North American standings with the 20 points he won at Devon. However, he is entered for next week’s World Cup qualifier in Mexico City.

The TerraNova success also boosted Devon and Vamos to third in the U.S. Open standings behind Kevin in first place and Canada’s Brittany Fraser-Beaulieu third. Ashley Holzer, also based in Welington, stands fourth. TerraNova was the last qualifier ahead of the final scheduled for Thermal, California next month.

Christian Simonson on Fleau de Baian, the 16-year-old Dutch-bred stallion he competed on the American team at the World Championships in Aachen, Germany in August, was runner-up Saturday on 73.670%.

Christian, also based in Wellington, was reserve champion on Indian Rock at the World Cup Final in Texas in April. His results at TerraNova moved him to fifth place in the U.S. Open standings.

James Koford on Fire Fly, the 16-year-old KWPN gelding he took over from Anna Marek a year ago, placed third on 72.910% in Saturday’s Freestyle.

World Cup qualifiers are in Mexico and Canada before returning to the U.S. to decide the three North Americans that will be invited to the championship Final scheduled for Gothenburg, Sweden at the end of March.

item.content:encoded:

Cathrine Laudrup-Dufour and the 17-year-old Mount St. John Freestyle captured the opening West European World Cup qualifier in Herning, Denmark Saturday, holding off a challenge from Holland’s Marieke van der Putten on Zantana Rs2 OLD.

Cathrine and Freestyle, a Hanoverian mare and both ranked world No. 1, were awarded 90.000% for the victory for three straight annual Wolrd Cup qualifier victories at this venue in the rider’s homeland of Denmark.

This has been a year in which Cathrine and Freestyle led Denmark to medals at the World Championships two months ago following medals at the Europeans in 2025 and the 2024 Olympics.years.

Marieke van der Putten and the 12-year-old Oldenburg mare Zantana Rs2 OLD scored a personal best 86.235% for runner-up as the pair was in the Grand Prix Friday.

However, the results showed significant disparities–a Danish judge awarded the pair the lowest score, 82.800%, while a second Danish judge gave them the second lowest score of 85.875%. Scores from the other three non-Danish judges ranged from 87.100% to 88.125%.

Sweden’s Maria von Essen on the 14-year-old Oldenburg gelding Invoice placed third on 81.475%.

The second of 10 West European qualifiers is scheduled for Lyon, France at the end of this month.

item.title: Devon Kane and Vamos Win TerraNova World Cup Grand Prix on Personal Best Score
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Devon Kane and Vamos win TerraNova World Cup Grand Prix on Personal Best Score

The post Devon Kane and Vamos Win TerraNova World Cup Grand Prix on Personal Best Score appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 16, 2026

Devon Kane and Vamos won the TerraNova World Cup Grand Prix on a personal best score Friday.

Devon and the 14-year-old Westfalen gelding scored 69.043% for the win on Florida’s Gulf Coast in extremely hot weather. The partnership of Devon and Vamos is nearing three years at Big Tour. Her family’s Diamante Farms of Wellington, Florida owns the horse.

A place in the top three–highly likely as there are only four in the musical freestyle Saturday–would put her atop the North American qualifying standings, knocking her husband Kevin Kohmann out of the leading position. This is the second of 10 World Cup qualifiers in North America leading to the final in Gothenburg, Sweden next March. Kevin won the circuit opener at Devon, Pennsylvania and is not competing here but entered in next week’s qualifier in Mexico City.

Christian Simonson on Fleau de Baian, the 16-year-old Dutch-bred stallion he competed on the U.S. team at the World Championships in August, was runner-up Saturday on 68.065%. Christian, also based in Wellington, was reserve champion on Indian Rock at the World Cup Final in Texas in April.

Quinn Iverson , also based in Wellington, rode the 11-year-old Oldenburg gelding Gremlin 41 to victory in the CDI3* Grand Prix on a personal best 69.696%.

Cathrine Laudrup-Dufour on Mount St. John Freestyle Clear Winner of Herning, Denmark World Cup Grand Prix Kicking Off West European Circuit for 2026-27 Championship

item.content:encoded:

Cathrine Laudrup-Dufour on Mount St. John Freestyle, both rider and horse ranked world No. 1, was a clear winner of the Herning, Denmark World Cup Grand Prix Friday to kick off the 10-event West European league for 2026-27 championship.

Cathrine and Freestyle were awarded 82.413% with all five judges marking the partnership above 80% and placing them atop the lineup of riders and horses from six nations, including Charlotte Jorst of the USA.

This has been a year in which Danish rider and the Hanoverian mare now 17 years old has posted their highest scores of her career beginning with 84.174% at this same stadium in March. The duo has led Denmark to medals at the World Championships two months ago , the 2025 Europeans and the 2024 Olympics.

Holland’s Marieke van der Putten on the 12-year-old Oldenburg mare Zantana Rs2 OLD was runner-up on 75.957%.

Daniel Bachmann Andersen, a Danish teammate of Cathrine, rode Flash Gordon, a 12-year-old Oldenburg gelding, to third place close behind on 75.652%.

The freestyle to decide points toward qualifying for the final in Gothenburg, Sweden next March is scheduled for Saturday.

item.title: Debbie McDonald’s Return to Coaching–Partly
item.dc:creator: StraightArrow
item.description:
Debbie McDonald's return to coaching after "retirement" a couple of years ago to help Morgan Klingensmith, stable rider for her friend Betsy Juliano

The post Debbie McDonald’s Return to Coaching–Partly appeared first on Dressage-News.
item.content:encoded:
Oct. 15, 2026

By KENNETH J. BRADDICK

Debbie McDonald has returned to coaching after “retirement” a couple of years ago to help Morgan Klingensmith, stable rider for her friend Elizabeth “Betsy Juliano.

Both one of the most successful riders in American dressage history and a coaching partner of USA team leader Robert Dover, Debbie describes her latest role as a “fill in” helping out Allison Brock as the regular trainer of Morgan on Betsy’s string of horses at Havensafe Farm in Wellington, Florida. Morgan is Debbie’s only student–online so far but might see her return to Wellington briefly to escape the snow in winter.

As a rider on the mare Brentina, Debbie led the U.S. to silver at the 2002 World Equestrian Games when German Olympic gold medalist Klaus Balkenhol was team coach (2001-2008), on the bronze medal team four years later, in 2003 became the first and still one of only two Americans to capture the World Cup as well as two Olympics including bronze in 2004.

She took on the official post of developing coach and worked within the “pipeline” created by Robert Dover to develop riders and horses from youngsters to top sport. Christine Traurig who was on the Sydney 2000 bronze medal team was named young horse coach at the time.

From the 2014 World Games, her own students made up significant numbers of the teams. Adrienne Lyle who had begun as a working student of Debbie’s years before had been on the 2012 Olympic team with Wizard and was back for 2014 along with team newcomer Laura Graves on Verdades. Two Years later at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, another of Debbie’s students, Kasey Perry-Glass on Dublet, joined Laura on Verdades and, along with Ali Brock on Rosevelt and Steffen Peters on Legolas claimed bronze after disappointments the previous two Games.

Debbie as the personal coach of three of the four riders on the Robert Dover-led squad captured silver at the WEG at home in Tryon in 2018 and, having succeeded Robert as coach, at the Tokyo Olympics followed with the first silver for U.S. dressage since the 1948 Olympics when there were only five team while the globe was still recovering from World War II.

“I love the fact that Betsy has given Morgan this opportunity because she has worked her butt off for years grooming, being there for Salvino and just 100% committed,” Debbie said. “She’s a decent rider. She’s got good feel and she’s a great student.”

As to the lineup of U.S. horses those of the three riders she was coaching during the peak years from 2014 to 2021 have retired.

A key to success at the time, she said, was teamwork.

“Robert and I were great together,” she recalled. “He was adamant about the team thing and he stuck to it and I stuck to it and it became a team. But you’re not a team if you’re not rooting for each other; if you’re just there for yourself, it’s not a team. And trust me, that goes a long way, team spirit.”

And she refers to the years when Klaus Balkenhol was coach and the U.S. teams included herself, Robert Dover, Günter Seidel, Steffen Peters and others “were always a team and helped each other in the warm ups. I mean, it was amazing. Not one of us was wishing they didn’t win if the other one did. You know, it was just pure team spirit.”

Another issue is that unlike previous periods in the U.S. as well as major dressage nations there have been separate coaches for different divisions, Christine Traurig has multiple responsibilities–team coach, young horses and developing though she has assistance from fellow Californian Günter and Olivia LaGoy-Weltz based on the East Coast.

“What country is their top coach doing all the stuff?’ Debbie questioned.

“You need really good people all the way down the line,” she said, “not that Christine isn’t good and can’t do the job. It’s an impossible job to do that and it’s really, really important for the developing. I mean the top is the top. They’re there. But the developing is really where it is.

“How is it possible to keep an eye on all the people who are in the developing squad and do the teams that you want to go to Aachen or wherever? Well, if you’ve got a developing coach working with riders coming up, those would not be going to Aachen, but they would probably go to lesser shows.”
